1. Core Clinical Tension: A 37-year-old asymptomatic woman on maintenance hemodialysis being evaluated for renal transplantation is incidentally found to have a multiloculated cystic left adnexal mass with mildly elevated CA-125 (39 U/mL). The core challenge lies in differentiating an ovarian epithelial neoplasm, endometrioma, or chronic tubo-ovarian abscess from isolated genital/adnexal mycobacterial disease in an immunocompromised host lacking pulmonary symptoms or active systemic signs.
2. Admission Breakpoint: Initial multimodal imaging (CT, transvaginal ultrasound, pelvic MRI), baseline tumor markers, and initial triage labs, immediately prior to TST/IGRA evaluation and diagnostic laparoscopy with tissue biopsy.
3. Differential Distinctions:
- Epithelial Ovarian Neoplasm / Malignancy: A multiloculated adnexal mass in the presence of elevated CA-125 (39 U/mL) in an ESRD patient creates high suspicion for ovarian cancer; however, HE4 was normal (70 pmol/L), ultrasound demonstrated thin septations with absent Doppler vascular flow, MRI showed lack of diffusion restriction, and histopathology confirmed granulomatous inflammation without malignancy.
- Endometrioma: Pelvic MRI revealed T1/T2 hyperintensity and fluid-fluid levels reminiscent of a chocolate cyst, but the patient was completely asymptomatic without dysmenorrhea, and laparoscopic biopsy demonstrated caseating granulomas rather than endometrial stroma and hemosiderin-laden macrophages.
- Tubo-Ovarian Abscess / Pelvic Inflammatory Disease: Multilocular adnexal collections commonly represent pelvic abscesses, but the patient had no fever, leukocytosis, pelvic tenderness, or Doppler hypervascularity.
case_prompt:
A 37-year-old woman (gravida 3, para 1) with regular menses and end-stage renal disease on maintenance hemodialysis three times weekly for 5 years underwent routine pre-kidney transplantation staging. She was entirely asymptomatic, denying pelvic pain, abnormal uterine bleeding, fever, chills, night sweats, or weight loss. Her past surgical history included a right adnexectomy for an ectopic pregnancy 4 years previously. She received Bacillus Calmette-Guérin vaccination in childhood and reported no known personal or family history of infectious lung disease.

On physical examination, she appeared well and was afebrile with a temperature of 36.8°C, blood pressure of 120/75 mmHg, pulse of 80 beats per minute, and body mass index of 21 kg/m^2. Her abdomen was soft, non-tender, and non-distended without ascites; a well-healed remote Pfannenstiel scar was present. Speculum and bimanual pelvic examinations were completely unremarkable.

Admission laboratory studies demonstrated baseline anemia of renal disease with a hemoglobin of 7.7 g/dL, absolute lymphocyte count of 600 /muL, C-reactive protein of 8 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 35 mm/h, and serum albumin of 34 g/L. Serum electrolytes were normal. Serum tumor markers revealed a mildly elevated CA-125 of 39 U/mL (reference: <35), normal human epididymis protein 4 (HE4) of 70 pmol/L, normal alpha-fetoprotein (3.56 ng/mL), normal carcinoembryonic antigen (4.25 ng/mL), and negative quantitative beta-hCG.

A staging CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis incidentally revealed a multiloculated cystic left adnexal mass measuring approximately 38 x 33 mm, with clear lung fields. Transvaginal pelvic ultrasonography confirmed a left adnexal multiloculated cystic lesion measuring 48 x 32 x 30 mm, displaying thin internal septations, absent internal color Doppler flow (resistance index > 0.8), and no solid vegetations. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a left ovarian cystic mass measuring 41 x 46 mm exhibiting T1 and T2 hyperintensity with an internal fluid-fluid level, with no abnormal contrast enhancement or diffusion restriction.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the multiloculated adnexal mass and elevated serum CA-125 (39 U/mL), but ruled out by normal HE4 (70 pmol/L), absence of Doppler vascularity or solid mural nodules on imaging, and histopathology showing granulomatous inflammation without malignant cells.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Differential diagnoses included endometrioma, tubo-ovarian abscess, and epithelial ovarian tumor. The absence of fever, normal tumor markers, lack of Doppler vascularity, and histologic proof helped exclude these entities.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Endometrioma was suspected based on MRI T1/T2 hyperintensity and fluid-fluid levels, while tubo-ovarian abscess was considered given the multiloculated cystic pelvic mass, but both were excluded by the absence of pelvic pain, normal Doppler vascular flow, and surgical pathology demonstrating caseating granulomas.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Differential diagnoses included endometrioma, tubo-ovarian abscess, and epithelial ovarian tumor.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Diagnostic laparoscopy and left ovarian cystectomy demonstrating thick-walled cysts with epithelioid granulomas, Langhans giant cells, and caseous necrosis, confirmed by positive Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast staining, positive Xpert MTB/RIF assay, and Lowenstein-Jensen culture growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Histopathology showed thickened fibrous cyst walls and epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells and caseous necrosis (Fig. 4).
